The Stone cockscomb (Alectrias alectrolophus) is a small, benthic marine fish inhabiting the rocky intertidal and subtidal zones of the North Pacific. Field surveys of adult specimens indicate that the maximum recorded total length for this species reaches 13 cm [Li = 13 cm], a size that places it among the smaller members of the Stichaeidae family. At the onset of reproductive maturation, individuals typically measure about 5 cm [Lp = about 5 cm] in total length, marking a distinct size threshold for the transition to adulthood. This pubertal size is reached after a period of juvenile growth that is strongly influenced by the thermal conditions of the local habitat. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the lifespan of Alectrias alectrolophus has been documented to extend to approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], a considerable longevity for such a diminutive fish and one that likely reflects the energetic constraints of its cold-water environment. Life history theory predicts that this combination of a moderate adult size and an extended lifespan would be paired with a relatively slow pace of reproduction.

Reproductive output in this species has been quantified through detailed spawning observations conducted under stable thermal regimes. When maintained at a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females produce an average of approximately 80 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 80 eggs per spawning event], and they typically complete a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year]. This annual reproductive strategy, with a single, moderately sized clutch, is characteristic of many iteroparous, temperate-zone stichaeids that invest in a small number of relatively large eggs. The restriction to a single, annual spawning bout, rather than multiple clutches across the season, suggests that the energy surplus available for gamete production is limited by the seasonal productivity of their benthic prey base. The eggs themselves are demersal and adhesive, deposited in a guarded nest within crevices or under boulders.

The initial investment per offspring is substantial for a fish of this size, as each newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight of just 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams]. This low body mass at birth, based on an egg diameter of approximately 1.7 mm, reflects the relatively large volume of yolk allocated to the embryo. The newly emerged prolarva is entirely lecithotrophic, relying on its endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance during the critical first days of life. During this yolk-sac larva stage, the alevin remains largely sedentary in the nest environment, absorbing yolk nutrients until the mouth opens and the transition to first exogenous feeding can occur. The timing of this trophic switch is critical, as the point of no return is reached if prey is not encountered soon after yolk-sac resorption is complete.

The extended developmental period and the species' overall slow life-history strategy are underscored by the maximum lifespan recorded. As noted, captive individuals have been recorded living up to 84 months [am = up to 84 months] at the same thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], underscoring the species' remarkable longevity for a fish of its size. This longevity is likely coupled with a delayed onset of reproduction, as maturity is not attained until a size of about 5 cm [Lp = about 5 cm] total length is reached. The combination of a long life, late maturity, and modest reproductive output per year implies a low intrinsic rate of population increase, making Alectrias alectrolophus potentially vulnerable to overexploitation or habitat disturbance. Comparative data from related stichaeid genera, such as Lumpenus and Anoplarchus, show that such life-history traits are common among cold-water, nest-guarding species.

In summary, the life history of the Stone cockscomb is characterized by a slow pace of life, with an ultimate total length of 13 cm [Li = 13 cm] representing the maximum size attainable through years of gradual somatic growth. The pubertal length of about 5 cm [Lp = about 5 cm] demarcates the transition to a reproductively viable individual, a milestone that is followed by a reproductive strategy delivering roughly 80 eggs in a single annual event [Ri = roughly 80 eggs in a single annual event] at the standard temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Each of these eggs yields a larva with a very low initial body mass of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a cost that is offset by the extended survival of the adults, who may live for up to 7 years [am = up to 7 years] under those same thermal conditions at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This suite of demographic parameters provides a valuable comparative baseline for understanding life-history variation among the cold-temperate fish fauna of the North Pacific.
